title: "refusing to merge unrelated histories"
summary: Someone initialised a new repository locally while the server already had one. The two share no commits at all. Understand why git refuses, then join them without losing either side.
mental_model: Merging needs a merge base — a commit both sides descend from. Two independently initialised repositories have none, so git refuses rather than inventing a base. The flag says 'treat the empty tree as the base', which is almost always a sign something went wrong earlier.

# Reef Controller

# Reef Controller

Started from scratch by mistake.

setup.run: sh -c 'git remote add origin ../origin.git && git fetch -q origin'

steps.title: See two histories that share nothing
steps.why: The local branch and origin/main each have their own root commit. There is no commit in common, which is exactly the condition git refuses to merge across.
steps.expect: Two root commits — the tell-tale sign.

verify.label: there are two independent root commits

steps.title: Confirm there is no merge base
steps.why: `merge-base` is the command git runs internally before merging. It returns nothing and exits non-zero — no shared ancestor, therefore no three-way merge is possible.
commands: sh -c 'git merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD origin/main; echo "is-ancestor exit: $?"'
steps.expect: No output and a non-zero exit — the mathematical reason for the refusal.

steps.title: Watch the refusal, and the push rejection
steps.why: Both operations fail for the same underlying reason. The error message is unusually clear about what git will not do, and unusually unclear about what you should do instead.
steps.expect: fatal: refusing to merge unrelated histories, then a non-fast-forward rejection.

steps.title: Consider the option people forget
steps.why: If the local repository has only a couple of commits, cloning properly and re-applying them by hand is cleaner than joining two roots. Reach for the flag only when the local history is genuinely worth keeping.
steps.expect: Two commits and two files — small enough that re-doing them would have been reasonable.

steps.title: Join them deliberately
steps.why: `--allow-unrelated-histories` tells git to use the empty tree as the base. Files present on one side only merge in cleanly; files on both sides — README.md here — conflict, because from the empty base both sides 'added' them.
steps.expect: An add/add conflict on README.md, and everything else merged.

verify.label: the shared file conflicts as an add/add

steps.title: Resolve and complete the merge
steps.why: Write the version that reflects reality — the server's project description — and finish. The result contains both sides' code and two root commits, which is unusual but perfectly valid.

steps.expect: Every file present, and HEAD reachable from two root commits.

steps.title: Push the joined history
steps.why: The branch now contains origin/main, so the push is an ordinary fast-forward. Nobody has to force anything, and no work was thrown away.

verify.label: the server has both histories joined
the server has the joined history
no work from either side was lost
the result legitimately has two root commits
the add/add conflict was resolved properly

pitfalls: The usual cause is `git init` in a directory that should have been a `git clone`. Check for that before merging anything.
Every file existing on both sides becomes an add/add conflict, because from an empty base both sides added it. On a large project that is hundreds of conflicts.
`--allow-unrelated-histories` was made non-default deliberately: the refusal catches a genuine mistake far more often than it obstructs a real need.
Two root commits confuse some tools and make `git log --graph` harder to read forever. If the local history is small, re-doing the work in a proper clone is often the better trade.
cheatsheet: the shared ancestor — empty means unrelated
